subject: Critical Thinking
title: Kant's Categorical Imperative: Act As If It Were Universal Law
description: A quick, practical guide to Kant's Categorical Imperative: Act As If It Were Universal Law.

hook.text: 'What if everyone did that?' Your mother's question is actually Immanuel Kant's most famous philosophical principle.

buildup.text: Kant's categorical imperative: act only according to rules you could will to be universal laws for everyone.

discovery.text: Test: 'Can I lie?' If everyone lied, trust collapses & lying becomes pointless.

twist.text: The problem: Kant says lying is ALWAYS wrong – even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding.

climax.text: Kant's lasting point is that moral rules must be consistent enough for everyone to live under them.

punchline.text: If you wouldn't want everyone to do it, you shouldn't do it either.

quiz.question: What does Kant's categorical imperative require?
options: Act only according to rules you could will to be universal laws for everyone

details.summary: Kant's categorical imperative demands that you act only according to principles you could will to become universal laws. It grounds morality in rational duty rather than outcomes or emotions.
details.whyItMatters: Kantian ethics provides a rigorous test for moral consistency that exposes self-serving exceptions people carve out for themselves.
takeaways: Moral rules must be universalizable without contradiction
Duty, not desire, is the foundation of ethical action
The test filters out self-serving exceptions

faq.question: How does the categorical imperative test whether an action is moral?
faq.answer: You ask whether the principle behind your action could become a universal rule without contradiction. If lying were universal, trust would collapse, making lying self-defeating.

faq.question: What is the main weakness of Kantian ethics?
faq.answer: It can produce rigid conclusions—like never lying, even to protect someone from a murderer—because it prioritizes duty over consequences in every case.
